extracted.subtask_description: Practical craft guidance for writing personal memoirs, covering memory, voice, truth, detail-selection, structure, revision, ethics, and tools for developing the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat Emptor
rubrics_metrics.description: Mary Karr emphasizes she does not represent all memoirists or every method; advice is drawn from her experience and conversations but is not a universal formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat craft guidance as one practitioner's approach. Avoid expecting a single prescriptive method — adapt principles to your own process.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Past’s Vigor (Memory’s Fallibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Memory is powerful, unpredictable, and often unreliable—like a pinball machine where fragments collide; emotional intensity and group narratives can distort recollection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge memory's malleability when using it as source material. Use corroborating sensory detail and documentary evidence where available; be skeptical of collective/retold family narratives and test memories (e.g., through classroom experiments or journals).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Truth Contract Twixt Writer and Reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Memoir creates a contract of truth with the reader; readers deserve to know the extent of embellishment and undisclosed fabrication breaches trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be transparent about reconstructions (e.g., reconstructed dialogue) and clearly signal fictionalized or uncertain elements. Anti-patterns: undisclosed fabrication, sensational falsehoods (cases cited: James Frey, Wilkomirski).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons to Reconsider Writing a Memoir / Emotional Readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing memoir is emotionally complex. Reasons to pause include heavy influence by others, poor memory, insufficient distance from events, being too young, writing purely for therapy or revenge, ongoing conflicts, and unwillingness to revise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-assess readiness (Karr’s pop quiz). Wait for adequate temporal distance (often suggested: ~7–8 years or after mid-30s if immature), ensure motives are not primarily revenge/therapy, and cultivate willingness to revise and accept potential backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing to Write — Meditative Practice & Sensory Focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Use centering/meditative exercises to quiet self-consciousness and foreground sensory impressions as a path to vivid memory recall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice focusing on smell, taste, touch, sight, and sound to generate concrete material; prefer sensory-driven recall over abstract summary. Anti-pattern: relying on intellectualization without embodied detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: A Voice Conjures the Human Who Utters It (Primacy of Voice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Voice is the essential element of memoir: it must feel authentic, balance humor and pathos, and conjure the human who speaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop voice across drafts; trust your unique perspective rather than mimicry. Strong voice fosters intimacy and reader trust. Examples: Frank Conroy, Frank McCourt. Scoring note: voice is often the first evaluator’s notice of quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Imitation of Another’s Ornate Style
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not imitate singular literary masters (e.g., Nabokov) at the cost of your own voice; ornate diction can alienate readers if it isn't genuinely yours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study admired writers but resist imitation. Use lessons from masters to inform, not to replace, your authentic idiom. Anti-pattern: adopting 'aristocratic' detachment that sacrifices emotional connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sacred Carnality (Use of Sensory / Totemic Details)
rubrics_metrics.description: Carnality—evoking physical sensations through the five senses—is crucial; totemic objects and tangible details lend credibility and emotional resonance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select concrete, specific, and unusual sensory details (totems) to ground scenes. Avoid generic descriptions that 'fall flat'; prefer particulars that produce a visceral response (examples: Chekhov's watermelon, Maya Angelou’s precise images).

rubrics_metrics.name: How to Choose a Detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose details that are vivid, trustable, and uniquely yours—details that conjure a scene and carry emotional truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate candidate details for concreteness, visual specificity, and emotional salience. Reject vague or ubiquitous details in favor of those that generate strong imagery and narrative function (Karr’s Mickey Heinz example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interiority and the 'Inner Enemy' (Private Agonies Over External Whammies)
rubrics_metrics.description: The engine of many memoirs is interior conflict—the 'inner enemy'—and moments of consciousness awakening; interiority often reads deeper than external events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center inner contradictions, guilt, shame, and self-questioning to generate narrative momentum. Vulnerability deepens reader engagement. Anti-pattern: overemphasizing external 'events' without psychic complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: On Finding the Nature of Your Talent / Authentic Self
rubrics_metrics.description: Talent in memoir grows from honest self-representation; confronting false selves and understanding how others perceive you helps locate your voice and material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use self-reflective questions (e.g., what do people like/dislike about you?) to map your strengths and blind spots. Be wary of presenting a polished persona that conceals the real subjectivity readers seek.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dealing with Beloveds (On and Off the Page)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write ethically about people you know: consider notifying family, weigh potential harm, and understand consequences of disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance candor with compassion; consider pseudonyms, timing, and conversations with those affected. Anti-patterns: careless dehumanizing language or writing primarily to wound others.

rubrics_metrics.name: On Information, Facts, and Data
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts and data can support memoir but must be woven into scenes and sensory detail rather than dumped as exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blend factual material into lived scenes; use data sparingly to illuminate rather than replace narrative. Avoid relying solely on 'data' to reveal character (anti-pattern referenced in quizzes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal Run-Ins with Fake Voices (Avoiding Persona)
rubrics_metrics.description: Early writers often hide authentic voice behind persona; discovery of one’s real voice is a turning point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work to strip artifice in drafts; let honesty and imperfection shape voice. Anti-pattern: clinging to a polished public persona that flattens interior life.

rubrics_metrics.name: On Book Structure and the Order of Information
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure—how you order scenes and reveal information—shapes meaning; memoirs need not be strictly linear and may employ flash-forwards or thematic arrangement to serve emotional truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think about narrative architecture: openings, reversals, and the placement of revelations. Use structure to deepen reader understanding rather than to merely transmit facts. Avoid arbitrary disorganization; structure should feel purposeful.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Road to Hell Is Paved with Exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggeration and sensationalism can damage credibility; emotional honesty is key.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize truthful emotional states over inflated drama. Check impulses to overdramatize; readers reward sincerity. Anti-patterns: exaggeration that undermines trust and invites scandal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blind Spots and False Selves
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers carry blind spots and constructed false selves shaped by social expectations; identifying and excavating these is essential to authentic memoir.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use revision and external feedback to locate blind spots. Be prepared to challenge self-flattering narratives and include scenes that complicate self-image rather than hide them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth Hunger — Public and Private Reckonings
rubrics_metrics.description: Memoirists grapple with both private compulsions and public appetite for sensational truth; cultural cynicism around truth necessitates disciplined honesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist market temptations to sensationalize. Emphasize ethical clarity and personal reckoning over performative disclosures. Learn from high-profile falsifications to maintain credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Old‑School Technologies for the Stalled Novice
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical tools for developing craft include keeping a commonplace book, memorizing poetry, and practicing close observation and short-form review writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt regular exercises: collect striking details, memorize lines to learn economy of language, write short criticism to sharpen judgment. Anti-pattern: expecting craft to arrive without disciplined practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why Memoirs Fail
rubrics_metrics.description: Common failure modes include lack of compelling voice, absence of interior change, poor selection of detail, weak structure, and insufficient revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use voice, interiority, specific detail, purposeful structure, and rigorous revision as corrective measures. Evaluate drafts against these axes to diagnose weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: An Incomplete Checklist to Stave Off Dread / Craft Habits
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of practical habits and standards: strive for clarity and brevity; read historical literature to develop taste; cultivate both a generative self and an editor self; approach revision with curiosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop taste by reading classics and biographies of writers; separate drafting (generative) from editing (editor); embrace revision as curiosity-driven discovery rather than punishment. Scoring note: revision often distinguishes good from great work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against Vanity: In Praise of Revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Revision is central to making work resilient and meaningful; the writer must endure self-doubt and persist through rigorous reworking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice iterative editing: reshape, cut, and clarify ruthlessly. View revision as the path to craft maturity; expect emotional challenges and use them productively. Learn from historical examples (e.g., Hemingway, G. H. Hardy) to reframe success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Michael Herr / Dispatches — Subjectivity of Truth and Stylistic Lessons
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples like Michael Herr demonstrate that reportage/memoir can privilege perception and emotional truth over strict chronology or factual completeness; humor and irony can coexist with horror.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider stylistic choices (fragmentation, voice blending, irony) to convey complexity of experience. Use such strategies with care—they serve expressive aims, not as cover for factual sloppiness.
